{{Short description|Theorem in projective geometry}}
[[File:Qvist-0-en.svg|250px|thumb|Qvist's theorem on finite ovals]]
In [[projective geometry]], '''Qvist's theorem''', named after the Finnish mathematician {{ill|Bertil Qvist|de}}, is a statement on [[Oval (projective plane)|oval]]s in ''finite'' [[projective plane]]s. Standard examples of ovals are non-degenerate [[Conic section|(projective) conic sections]]. The theorem gives an answer to the question ''How many tangents to an oval can pass through a point in a finite projective plane?'' The answer depends essentially upon the [[Projective plane#Finite projective planes|order]] (number of points on a line −1) of the plane.

== Definition of an oval ==
{{main article|Oval (projective plane)}}
*In a [[projective plane]] a set {{math|Ω}} of points is called an '''oval''', if:
# Any line {{mvar|l}} meets {{math|Ω}} in at most two points, and
# For any point {{math|''P'' ∈ Ω}} there exists exactly one tangent line {{mvar|t}} through {{mvar|P}}, i.e., {{math|1=''t'' ∩ Ω = {''P''}}}.

When {{math|1={{abs|''l'' ∩ Ω }} = 0}} the line {{mvar|l}} is an ''exterior line'' (or ''passant''),<ref>In the English literature this term is usually rendered in French (or German) rather than translating it as a passing line.</ref> if {{math|1={{abs|''l'' ∩ Ω}} = 1}} a ''tangent line'' and if {{math|1={{abs|''l'' ∩ Ω}} = 2}} the line is a ''secant line''.

For ''finite'' planes (i.e. the set of points is finite) we have a more convenient characterization:<ref>{{harvnb|Dembowski|1968|page=147}}</ref>
* For a finite projective plane of ''order'' {{mvar|n}} (i.e. any line contains {{math|''n'' + 1}} points) a set {{math|Ω}} of points is an oval [[if and only if]] {{math|1={{abs|Ω}} = ''n'' + 1}} and no three points are [[collinear]] (on a common line).

== Statement and proof of Qvist's theorem ==
;Qvist's theorem<ref>Bertil Qvist: ''Some remarks concerning curves of the second degree in a finite plane'', Helsinki (1952), Ann. Acad. Sci Fenn Nr. 134, 1–27</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Dembowski|1968|pages=147–8}}</ref>
Let {{math|Ω}} be an oval in a finite projective plane of order {{mvar|n}}.
:(a) If {{mvar|n}} is ''odd'',
::every point {{math|''P'' ∉ Ω}} is incident with 0 or 2 tangents.
:(b) If {{mvar|n}} is ''even'',
::there exists a point {{mvar|N}}, the ''nucleus'' or ''knot'', such that, the set of tangents to oval {{math|Ω}} is the pencil of all lines through {{mvar|N}}.
[[File:Qvist-theorem-a-en.svg|250px|thumb|Qvist's theorem: to the proof in case of n odd]]
[[File:Qvist-theorem-b-en.svg|250px|thumb|Qvist's theorem: to the proof in case of n even]]
;Proof:
(a) Let {{math|''t''<sub>''R''</sub>}} be the tangent to {{math|Ω}} at point {{mvar|R}} and let {{math|''P''<sub>1</sub>, ... , ''P''<sub>''n''</sub>}} be the remaining points of this line. For each {{math|i}}, the lines through {{math|''P''<sub>''i''</sub>}} partition {{math|Ω}} into sets of cardinality 2 or 1 or 0. Since the number {{math|1={{abs|Ω}} = ''n'' + 1}} is even, for any point {{math|''P''<sub>''i''</sub>}}, there must exist at least one more tangent through that point. The total number of tangents is {{math|''n'' + 1}}, hence, there are exactly two tangents through each {{math|''P''<sub>i</sub>}}, {{math|''t''<sub>''R''</sub>}} and one other. Thus, for any point {{mvar|P}} not in oval {{math|Ω}}, if {{mvar|P}} is on any tangent to {{math|Ω}} it is on exactly two tangents.

(b) Let {{mvar|s}} be a secant, {{math|1=''s'' ∩ Ω = {''P''<sub>0</sub>, ''P''<sub>1</sub>}}} and {{math|1=''s''= {''P''<sub>0</sub>, ''P''<sub>1</sub>,...,''P''<sub>n</sub>}}}. Because {{math|1={{abs|Ω}} = ''n'' + 1}} is odd, through any {{math|1=''P''<sub>''i''</sub>, i = 2,...,n}}, there passes at least one tangent {{math|''t''<sub>i</sub>}}. The total number of tangents is {{math|''n'' + 1}}. Hence, through any point {{math|''P''<sub>''i''</sub>}} for {{math|1=i = 2,...,''n''}} there is exactly one tangent. If {{mvar|N}} is the point of intersection of two tangents, no secant can pass through {{mvar|N}}. Because {{math|''n'' + 1}}, the number of tangents, is also the number of lines through any point, any line through {{mvar|N}} is a tangent.

; Example in a pappian plane of even order:
Using [[Homogeneous coordinates|inhomogeneous coordinates]] over a field {{math|1=''K'',  {{abs|''K''}} = ''n''}} even, the set
:{{math|1=Ω<sub>1</sub> = {(''x, y'') {{!}} ''y'' = ''x''<sup>2</sup>} ∪ {(∞)}}},
the projective closure of the parabola {{math|1=''y'' = ''x''<sup>2</sup>}}, is an oval with the point {{math|1=''N'' = (0)}} as nucleus (see image), i.e., any line {{math|1=''y'' = ''c''}}, with {{math|''c'' ∈ ''K''}}, is a tangent.

== Definition and property of hyperovals ==
*Any oval {{math|Ω}} in a ''finite'' projective plane of ''even'' order {{mvar|n}} has a nucleus {{mvar|N}}.

:The point set {{math|1={{overline|Ω}} := Ω ∪ {''N''}}} is called a '''[[hyperoval]]''' or ({{math|''n'' + 2}})-''arc''. (A finite oval is an ({{math|''n'' + 1}})-''arc''.)

One easily checks the following essential property of a hyperoval:
*For a hyperoval {{math|{{overline|Ω}}}} and a point {{math|''R'' ∈ {{overline|Ω}}}} the pointset {{math|{{overline|Ω}} \ {''R''}}} is an oval.
[[File:Proj-kegs-parab-s.svg|250px|thumb|projective conic section {{math|Ω<sub>1</sub>}}]]

This property provides a simple means of constructing additional ovals from a given oval.

;Example:
For a projective plane over a [[finite field]]  {{math|1=''K'', {{abs|''K''}} = ''n''}} even and {{math|''n'' > 4}}, the set
: {{math|1=Ω<sub>1</sub> = {(''x, y'') {{!}} ''y'' = ''x''<sup>2</sup>} ∪ {(∞)}}} is an oval (conic section) (see image),
: {{math|1={{overline|Ω}}<sub>1</sub> = {(''x, y'') {{!}} ''y'' = ''x''<sup>2</sup>} ∪ {(0), (∞)}}} is a hyperoval and
: {{math|1=Ω<sub>2</sub> = {(''x, y'') {{!}} ''y'' = ''x''<sup>2</sup>} ∪ {(0)}}} is another oval that is not a conic section. (Recall that a conic section is determined uniquely by 5 points.)
